title: TWA 277

location.name: Fort Mountain, Maine's Baxter State Park

summary: TWA Flight 277, a C-54 Skymaster en route from Stephenville, Newfoundland to Washington, D.C., encountered severe weather on 20 June 1944 including heavy rains, high winds, and lightning-induced radio static over New Brunswick and Maine. The aircraft was blown 70 miles off course. The pilot apparently did not realize the aircraft, flying at less than 4,000 feet, had been blown into mountainous territory with peaks in excess of 5,000 feet. The aircraft's starboard wing struck a ridge of boulders at an elevation of 3700 feet on Fort Mountain.
probable_cause: Navigation error and spatial disorientation in severe weather

title: Long Creek Air Tragedy Memorial
summary: A-26 Invader piloted by Second Lieutenant Philip Irvin Russell descended toward Portland airport in patchy heavy fog on a long-range training mission from Barksdale. Portland airport had closed at 16:35 due to fog. The pilot requested landing; the controller instructed him to climb to 1500 ft, but he descended and struck the ground in a trailer park at low altitude. The aircraft cartwheeled through 16 trailers, killing the pilot and navigator and 17 residents; 20 residents were injured.
probable_cause: The pilot lacked experience flying this aircraft on instruments. An operations officer signed a form indicating CFR when conditions required IFR. The controller suggested a runway instead of advising the pilot to return to VFR conditions.

title: Freckleton Air Disaster
summary: At approximately 10:36 on 23 August 1944, two newly refurbished B-24 aircraft departed Base Air Depot No. 2 on scheduled test flights. Test pilot First Lieutenant John Bloemendal was flying an aircraft designated Classy Chassis II. The pilots flew north at low altitude and encountered a violent incoming thunderstorm with reduced visibility. Both pilots were ordered to land at once at 10:41 a.m. First Lieutenant Bloemendal, flying at low altitude with reduced visibility, began struggling against violent turbulence and ordered his co-pilot to gain altitude. The aircraft crashed into the centre of the village of Freckleton, Lancashire, killing all three crewmen and 58 individuals on the ground, including 38 children. An official inquiry was unable to pinpoint an exact cause but noted the report was unable to discount structural failure in extreme weather conditions.
probable_cause: An official inquiry was unable to pinpoint an exact cause for the accident, although the report was unable to discount structural failure of the aircraft in such extreme weather conditions as a factor for the accident.

title: 1944 Neuleiningen Douglas DC-3 shootdown
summary: On 24 September 1944, a Royal Canadian Air Force Douglas C-47 Dakota on a military transport mission departed RAF Pershore and encountered poor weather. The aircraft veered off course into German airspace and was attacked by a Luftwaffe Messerschmitt Bf 109 piloted by Julius Meimberg. The fighter fired at the right engine and the C-47 entered a split S maneuver, but the wing separated in flight. The aircraft crashed near Neuleiningen with all 23 occupants killed.

title: 1944 Hochdahl-Trills Handley Page Halifax shootdown
summary: A Handley Page Halifax bomber from No. 408 Squadron RCAF was attacked by a German Messerschmitt Bf 110 G-4 night fighter shortly after releasing its payload near the target. The night fighter pilot Hauptmann Fritz Lau approached from the rear, hit the bomber and set it on fire. The aircraft flew a few more kilometers before exploding midair at 19:10 over Hochdahl-Trills. Three crew members survived after bailing out; five were killed. Flight Lieutenant Albert Edward Steeves was hospitalized in Haan before being sent to Stalag Luft I, and Sergeant James Alexander McPhee evaded capture for six days before being handed over to police. Pilot Officer Edmond Kenneth Wilson died in a POW hospital in Düsseldorf that evening; five other crew members died near the crash site.
probable_cause: Attack by German Messerschmitt Bf 110 G-4 night fighter from IV./Nachtjagdgeschwader 1 under pilot Hauptmann Fritz Lau, which hit the bomber and set it afire during the return flight from bombing Castrop-Rauxel.
